lessons.title: AI Data Centers and the Grid: Who Pays, Who Decides?
lessons.question: Who pays, who decides, and what changes when AI data centers connect to local electricity grids?
lessons.whyItMayMatter: The same physical load appears differently as a technical reliability problem, a utility investment, a ratepayer cost, a local development bargain and a public-governance decision.

lessons.title: Climate Risk and Housing: How Maps, Insurance, and Mortgages Decide Who Pays
lessons.question: How do climate hazards become unequal housing costs through maps, insurance, and mortgages?
lessons.whyItMayMatter: A physical hazard becomes a household price through risk models, map boundaries, insurance underwriting, mortgage requirements, regulatory choices and unequal capacity to absorb loss.

lessons.title: Lithium for Batteries: Who Gets the Water, Jobs, and Costs?
lessons.question: How does lithium extraction for batteries distribute water use, economic benefits, and decision-making power between mining regions and the wider energy transition?
lessons.whyItMayMatter: Battery supply chains connect climate goals and consumer technologies to local water systems, Indigenous and community rights, mine workers, public subsidies, and decisions over who bears environmental costs.

lessons.question: How do different waste management strategies distribute environmental costs, economic benefits, and decision-making power between local communities and the wider public health and environmental systems?
lessons.title: Waste Management: Who Bears the Costs, Who Decides?
lessons.whyItMayMatter: A waste disposal method appears differently as a technical reliability problem, a municipal cost, a community health risk, a regulatory compliance issue, and a long-term environmental liability.

purpose: Explain relations among social, technical, and economic systems, making practical stakes legible without flattening uncertainty.
